652.title: Indrajit's death
652.hook: Indrajit kills Sita in front of Hanuman, or seems to
652.howItsDone: Some Ramayana tellers use the illusory Sita, the māyā-sītā of this episode, to talk about māyā, illusion, and how fear can make what is false look real.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the mountain of herbs, and how two flights became one picture on shrine walls. Did you send a message of care? A new week begins, and Indrajit tries his cruelest trick. Day six hundred fifty-two.

Indrajit rides out of Lanka's western gate with a woman in his chariot. She's thin, in a soiled garment, weeping, calling Rama's name. Hanuman sees her and freezes. He's the one who sat in the tree above her in the ashoka grove. He knows that face. It's Sita. And in front of the whole monkey army, Indrajit seizes her by the hair, draws his sword, and cuts her down. Then he shouts across the field: there's nothing left to fight for now.
screen: `A WOMAN IN THE CHARIOT.` → `HANUMAN FREEZES.` → `NOTHING LEFT TO FIGHT FOR.`

segments.voice: Hanuman, the one who crossed the sea to find her, pulls the army back in despair and goes to tell Rama. And Rama, hearing it, collapses. Lakshmana holds him and, in grief, rails against a world where doing right seems to bring only suffering. Then Vibhishana arrives, and he's the one person in the camp who knows how Lanka thinks. That wasn't Sita, he says. Ravana would never allow her to be killed; he wants her too much. It was an illusion, a magic double. And it was a distraction. Right now, Indrajit is on his way to Nikumbhila, a sacred grove and shrine, to complete a fire offering. If he finishes it, he'll be unbeatable. But Brahma's boon has a condition: whoever attacks him there, before the rite is done, can kill him. So, Vibhishana says, send Lakshmana now. Notice what Indrajit has done. He didn't need to win a battle. He needed a few hours, and he knew exactly what would stop his enemies cold: the sight of the person they love most, dying. It's a cruel weapon, because it doesn't touch the body. It goes straight for the heart, and for a while it works. What breaks the spell isn't strength. It's a calm voice that knows the enemy, saying: look again; this isn't what it seems. Rama, steadied, sends Lakshmana off with Vibhishana, Hanuman and an army. The race to Nikumbhila begins.
screen: `RAMA COLLAPSES.` · `VIBHISHANA: IT WAS AN ILLUSION.` · `THE FIRE AT NIKUMBHILA.` · `A WEAPON AIMED AT THE HEART.` · then, large: `LOOK AGAIN; IT ISN'T WHAT IT SEEMS.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your breathing slow. Think of a fear that has gripped you lately, a picture your mind showed you of something terrible happening. Notice how real it felt. Now picture Vibhishana's calm voice beside you, saying: look again. What do you actually know? Breathe in, and separate the picture from the facts. Breathe out, and let the picture fade a little. The bell holds the time.
Indrajit's death. It begins with his cruelest trick, a magic Sita cut down before the army, and Vibhishana seeing through it to the fire at Nikumbhila.
Your line: Indrajit's death. Today, when fear paints a picture, ask what you actually know. Day six hundred fifty-two.

trapdoor: what you thought: Indrajit was just a strong warrior.
what it means: his worst weapon here is an illusion aimed at the heart, to buy time for his rite.

653.title: Indrajit's death
653.hook: an uncle and a nephew face each other at the fire, and Lakshmana makes a vow on his brother's name
653.howItsDone: Lakshmana's vow before the final arrow, resting on Rama's righteousness and truth, is often quoted by Ramayana teachers as a picture of Lakshmana's devotion to his brother.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Indrajit's death began with an illusion, a magic Sita cut down to stop the army, and Vibhishana saying look again. Did you separate a fear from the facts? Today, the race reaches Nikumbhila. Day six hundred fifty-three.

The grove at Nikumbhila is dark with trees, and somewhere inside, a fire is burning. Lakshmana's army crashes into the rakshasas guarding it, and the fighting gets so loud and close that Indrajit has to leave his offering unfinished and come out. He climbs into his chariot. And the first face he sees in the enemy line isn't Lakshmana's. It's his uncle's. Vibhishana, who knew about the fire, and the grove, and the secret condition, and who brought them here.
screen: `THE FIRE IN THE GROVE.` → `THE RITE LEFT UNFINISHED.` → `HIS UNCLE'S FACE.`

segments.voice: Indrajit's words to Vibhishana are bitter. You were born here, he says, you're my father's brother, and you've brought the enemy to your own nephew. You've thrown away your family and your people to serve strangers. Vibhishana answers without shouting. I was born among the rakshasas, he says, but my nature isn't cruel. I left my brother because of what he was doing: carrying off another man's wife, harming those who had done him no wrong. I couldn't take part in it. Both of them are speaking from loyalty; they just mean different things by it. Then the duel begins, Lakshmana and Indrajit, and Valmiki makes it long and close: chariots wrecked, armor split, both men bleeding, neither giving way. At last Lakshmana fits to his bow the weapon of Indra, the king of the gods. And before he lets it go, he speaks a vow. If Rama, son of Dasharatha, is righteous, and true to his word, and unmatched in courage, then let this arrow kill Ravana's son. The arrow flies, and Indrajit falls. Listen to the shape of that vow. Lakshmana doesn't rest the arrow on his own strength. He rests it on his brother's goodness. And the warrior named conqueror of Indra is brought down, at last, by Indra's own weapon. In Lanka, Ravana hears and loses his mind with grief. He grabs his sword and rushes toward the ashoka grove to kill Sita. A minister named Suparshva steps in front of him. You, a learned king, would kill a woman? Fight Rama instead. Ravana turns back.
screen: `YOU BETRAYED YOUR FAMILY.` · `MY NATURE ISN'T CRUEL.` · `A VOW ON RAMA'S GOODNESS.` · `SUPARSHVA STOPS THE SWORD.` · then, large: `BROUGHT DOWN BY INDRA'S OWN WEAPON.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Think of someone whose goodness you trust completely. A parent, a teacher, a friend. Lakshmana put his whole weight on his brother's goodness. Picture this person, and let yourself lean on them for a moment, in your mind. Breathe in their steadiness. Breathe out, and let whatever you're facing rest on that steadiness for a moment. The bell holds the time.
Indrajit's death. At Nikumbhila, his rite broken, he falls to Lakshmana's arrow of Indra, shot on a vow resting on Rama's goodness.
Your line: Indrajit's death. Today, lean on one person whose goodness you trust, and tell them. Day six hundred fifty-three.

654.title: Ravana's final battle
654.hook: a spear meant for Vibhishana, a brother who steps in front of it, and a chariot sent from heaven
654.howItsDone: Ramlila performances across North India build toward Ravana's final battle over many nights. Many follow Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas, where the wounding of Lakshmana that audiences know best comes earlier, from Meghnad (Indrajit), and Sushena and Hanuman's mountain save him there.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Indrajit's death, at Nikumbhila, by Indra's own weapon, on a vow resting on Rama's goodness. Did you lean on someone you trust? Today, with his son gone, Ravana rides out for the last time. Day six hundred fifty-four.

Ravana has no one left to send. His brother Kumbhakarna is dead. His son Indrajit is dead. Most of his champions are gone. So he puts on his armor, mounts his great chariot, and rides out through the gates himself, with whatever army remains. The monkeys scatter before him. And in the enemy line he sees the brother who left him, Vibhishana. Ravana picks up a great spear, made to kill, and aims it at him.
screen: `NO ONE LEFT TO SEND.` → `RAVANA RIDES OUT.` → `A SPEAR AIMED AT VIBHISHANA.`

segments.voice: Lakshmana sees it, and he doesn't hesitate. He fires at Ravana again and again, drawing his attention away from Vibhishana. Remember Rama's vow on the beach: anyone who comes for refuge is safe. Lakshmana is keeping it with his own body. Ravana, furious, turns the spear on him. You saved him, he says, so take this instead. The spear strikes Lakshmana in the chest, and he falls. Rama pulls the spear out and breaks it, and then, Valmiki says, he sits by his brother and weeps. What would I do with victory, with Sita even, without Lakshmana? In Valmiki this is where the second herb flight comes. Sushena, the monkey physician, kneels and looks at Lakshmana's face. He isn't dead, he says; his face hasn't changed. He sends Hanuman to a mountain for herbs, and once more Hanuman comes back carrying a whole peak. Sushena crushes a herb and holds it to Lakshmana's nose, and he breathes it in and gets up. And now something else arrives from the sky. Rama has been fighting on foot this whole war, against a king in a chariot. The gods see it, and Indra sends his own chariot down to Rama, with his charioteer, Matali, holding the reins. Matali bows. This chariot is yours, he says. Rama walks around it with respect, and climbs aboard. For the first time, the two of them meet as equals: Ravana in his chariot, Rama in Indra's. The last battle can begin.
screen: `LAKSHMANA KEEPS RAMA'S VOW.` · `THE SPEAR STRIKES LAKSHMANA.` · `SUSHENA AND THE SECOND HERB.` · `INDRA'S CHARIOT AND MATALI.` · then, large: `FOR THE FIRST TIME, AS EQUALS.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your breath slow. Think of a promise someone close to you made, one you could help them keep: a parent's promise, a friend's commitment, a team's word. Lakshmana kept his brother's vow without being asked. Picture one small way you could help. Hold it in mind. Breathe in, and feel steady. Breathe out, and feel ready. The bell holds the time.
Ravana's final battle. It begins with a spear aimed at Vibhishana, Lakshmana stepping into its path, Sushena's herb, and Indra's chariot sent down for Rama.
Your line: Ravana's final battle. Today, help someone keep a promise they made, without being asked. Day six hundred fifty-four.

655.title: Ravana's final battle
655.hook: a sage with a hymn to the sun, heads that grow back, and one last arrow
655.howItsDone: Devotees recite the Aditya Hridayam, especially at sunrise, and on Dussehra (Vijayadashami) Ramlila performances in North India end with Ravana's effigy being burned.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ravana's final battle began. Lakshmana took a spear meant for Vibhishana, Sushena's herb brought him back, and Indra's chariot came down for Rama. Did you help someone keep a promise? Today, the end of the war. Day six hundred fifty-five.

The duel has gone on so long that Rama is worn out. He stands in Indra's chariot, thinking, tired to the bone, with Ravana in front of him ready to fight again. And in that pause, Valmiki says, the sage Agastya, who had come with the gods to watch, walks up to Rama on the battlefield. Agastya, the same sage who gave Rama weapons years ago in the forest. This time he doesn't bring a weapon. He brings a hymn.
screen: `WORN OUT.` → `AGASTYA WALKS UP.` → `NOT A WEAPON. A HYMN.`

segments.voice: It's called the Aditya Hridayam, the heart of the sun, a hymn in praise of the sun as the source of light and life. Agastya teaches it to Rama there and then, and tells him to recite it three times. Rama does, facing the sun, and Valmiki says his weariness lifts and his heart fills with courage. The hymn is still recited today, often at sunrise, and some reach for it in exhausting stretches of their own lives. Then the fight resumes, and it's terrifying. Rama cuts off one of Ravana's heads with an arrow, and another grows in its place. He cuts that one off, and another grows. Again and again, Valmiki says, a hundred times. Ravana can't be ended this way. Matali, the charioteer, leans over and reminds Rama of something he's been carrying all along: the weapon of Brahma, given to him long ago by the sage Agastya. Rama takes it up. It blazes, Valmiki says, like the fire at the end of time. He charges it with the proper mantra, draws his bow to the full, and lets it go. The arrow strikes Ravana in the chest, and he falls from his chariot. Then it returns, the text says, to Rama's quiver. The gods rain flowers. The monkeys roar. Vibhishana stands over his fallen brother. On Dussehra, also called Vijayadashami, towns in North India set giant effigies of Ravana alight to mark this victory. In the book, the moment is quieter: a tired man, a hymn to the sun, and one arrow.
screen: `THE HEART OF THE SUN.` · `HEADS THAT GROW BACK.` · `MATALI: THE BRAHMA WEAPON.` · `RAVANA FALLS.` · then, large: `A TIRED MAN, A HYMN, ONE ARROW.`

segments.voice: Sit, and if you can, turn toward a window or wherever the sun is today. Notice any tiredness honestly, the way Rama faced his. Then imagine light on your face. Breathe in, as if breathing in that light. Breathe out the weariness. If you pray, you might offer a few words of thanks to the sun in your own way. Simply resting in light is enough. The bell holds the time.
Ravana's final battle. Agastya's hymn to the sun lifts Rama's weariness, Ravana's heads keep growing back, and the weapon of Brahma ends the war.
Your line: Ravana's final battle. Today, when you're tired to the bone, step into the light for one minute before the next thing. Day six hundred fifty-five.

656.title: Mandodari
656.hook: Ravana's queen walks onto the battlefield, and says what no one else could say
656.howItsDone: Some Hindus recite a traditional verse naming five revered women of the epics, the pañcakanyā, with Mandodari among them, and some say it in the morning; versions differ on one of the names.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ravana's final battle. A hymn to the sun, heads that grew back, and the weapon of Brahma. Did you step into the light when you were tired? Today, the war is over, and someone comes out of the city to grieve. Day six hundred fifty-six.

When the noise of victory dies down, the gates of Lanka open, and the women of Ravana's palace come out onto the battlefield. They've lost husbands, sons, brothers. They walk among the dead, weeping, until they find him. And one of them comes forward to the body and kneels. She is Mandodari, Ravana's chief queen, Indrajit's mother. She has lost her son, and now her husband. Valmiki lets her speak over him at length.
screen: `THE GATES OPEN.` → `THE WOMEN COME OUT.` → `MANDODARI KNEELS.`

segments.voice: Her lament holds love and truth at the same time. She remembers who he was. You frightened the gods, she says. Indra himself feared you. The earth and the mountains trembled at your name. How could a man on foot, wandering in the forest, bring you down? And then she answers her own question, in two ways. First she says Rama can't be only a man. In Valmiki's words as she grieves, he must be the eternal, the supreme, Vishnu himself, come in human form. A queen of Lanka is the one who says it out loud, over her husband's body. Then she turns to Ravana's own part in it, gently and without flinching. Long ago, she says, you conquered your senses, and with that discipline you conquered the three worlds. Now, it's as if your senses remembered and took their revenge. Your desire for Sita did what no army could. She says she warned him. She says Sita's faithfulness was a fire he couldn't hold. And then she simply grieves: her husband, her son, her life in pieces. She falls across his chest and weeps. Later tradition honored her. A well-known Sanskrit verse names five women of the epics whose remembrance is said to wash away wrongdoing, and Mandodari is one of them. Valmiki's portrait suggests why. She's loyal without being blind. She sees her husband whole, the greatness and the ruin, and she mourns him anyway.
screen: `YOU FRIGHTENED THE GODS.` · `RAMA IS MORE THAN A MAN.` · `YOUR SENSES TOOK REVENGE.` · `ONE OF THE FIVE WOMEN.` · then, large: `LOYAL WITHOUT BEING BLIND.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your breath be soft. Think of someone you love who has real faults, maybe someone you've lost. Let yourself see them whole, as Mandodari did: what was great in them, and what went wrong. Don't argue with either. Hold both in the same breath. Breathe in with the love. Breathe out with the honesty. Let them sit together. The bell holds the time.
Mandodari. Ravana's chief queen and Indrajit's mother, who grieves him on the battlefield, naming both his greatness and the desire that destroyed him.
Your line: Mandodari. Today, remember one person whole, the good and the hard, with love. Day six hundred fifty-six.

and that his desire for Sita was their revenge.

657.title: Mandodari
657.hook: after Mandodari's grief, a funeral, a coronation, and two acts of mercy
657.howItsDone: Rama's words that enmity ends at death (maraṇāntāni vairāṇi) and Sita's mercy toward her guards are quoted by Hindu teachers on forgiveness and on treating the dead with respect.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Mandodari, kneeling by Ravana, naming his greatness and his fault in the same breath. Did you remember someone whole? Today, what happens after her grief: who will give the king his last rites? Day six hundred fifty-seven.

Mandodari's lament ends. The other women lift her gently and lead her back toward the city. And Ravana's body is still lying on the field. Someone has to perform his funeral rites, and by custom that duty falls to his closest kin. That's Vibhishana. But Vibhishana stands back. He tells Rama he can't do it. This man was cruel, he says, he wronged others' wives, he was against everything right. How can I honor him?
screen: `MANDODARI LED HOME.` → `A KING STILL ON THE FIELD.` → `VIBHISHANA STANDS BACK.`

segments.voice: Rama's answer is short, and it is still quoted. Enmity ends at death. Our purpose is finished. Perform his rites. He is mine now, as much as he is yours. Think about who's saying this: the man whose wife Ravana stole, whose brother Ravana nearly killed. The moment the war is over, Rama refuses to carry the hatred one step further. Ravana was a great warrior, he says, and he deserves a king's funeral. So Vibhishana does it, with fire and ritual, as a brother. Mandodari's grief and Rama's command fit together. She saw Ravana whole; Rama lets him be honored whole. Then Rama has Vibhishana crowned king of Lanka, properly this time, and sends Hanuman into the city with the news for Sita. That gives us a second mercy. Hanuman finds Sita in the grove, surrounded by the rakshasi guards who threatened her for months. He tells her Ravana is dead, and she's too moved to speak. Then he offers, angrily, to kill every one of the guards. Sita stops him. They were servants following a king's orders, she says. And then, in Valmiki, she says something that sounds like a whole teaching. A noble person shows compassion to the guilty and the good alike, because no one is without fault. Two people with every reason for revenge, Rama and Sita, on the same day, both refuse it.
screen: `ENMITY ENDS AT DEATH.` · `HE IS MINE AS MUCH AS YOURS.` · `HANUMAN BRINGS SITA THE NEWS.` · `NO ONE IS WITHOUT FAULT.` · then, large: `TWO REFUSALS OF REVENGE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Bring to mind an old conflict that's really over: a job you left, a relationship that ended, a fight from years ago. Notice if you're still carrying some of the anger. You don't have to forgive anything right now. Just try Rama's sentence, quietly, for this one: it's over. Breathe in. Breathe out, and set one ounce of it down. The bell holds the time.
Mandodari. After her lament, Ravana is given a king's funeral by Rama's command, and Sita refuses revenge on the guards who tormented her.
Your line: Mandodari. Today, let one finished fight be finished, and stop carrying it into new rooms. Day six hundred fifty-seven.

658.title: the fire
658.hook: the reunion everyone has waited for, and the hardest words in the epic
658.howItsDone: Hindu teachers, scholars and storytellers discuss this scene from many sides, and some retellings, including women's songs and regional Ramayanas, give Sita's side of it at length.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Mandodari's grief, then Rama's words, enmity ends at death, and Sita sparing her guards. Did you let a finished fight be finished? Today, the reunion, and the week closes. Day six hundred fifty-eight.

For months, everything in this story has pointed to one moment. The search parties, the leap, the ring, the jewel, the bridge, the war. Now Vibhishana brings Sita out of the grove, bathed and dressed in fine clothes, carried toward Rama through a crowd of monkeys and rakshasas pressing to see her. Rama says: let her walk, so everyone can see. She steps down and walks toward him, shy and full of joy, looking at his face. And what happens next has troubled readers, inside the tradition and out.
screen: `EVERYTHING POINTED HERE.` → `SITA WALKS TOWARD HIM.` → `WHAT HAPPENS NEXT.`

segments.voice: Rama does not take her in his arms. In Valmiki he speaks coldly, in front of everyone. I've won you back, he says, and I've wiped out the insult to my family's name. But know this: I didn't fight this war for you. I fought it for my honor and my family's. Then he says the words that hurt most. She lived in another man's house for a long time. He doesn't feel he can take her back. She's free to go wherever she likes, he says, and he even names men she could go to. Valmiki doesn't soften it. The text says Sita weeps, ashamed in front of the crowd, shrinking as if into herself, and that those watching are shaken too. It's a hard passage, and people within the tradition have argued about it for a long time. Some teachers say Rama is speaking as a king, not a husband: a king must be seen to be beyond suspicion, and he's performing for his people, not speaking from his heart. Some read it as a test meant for the world rather than for Sita. Other readers, Hindu and not, find it simply wrong, and say so, and side with Sita. The epic has room for all those readers. Tomorrow, Sita answers. And so a week that began with an illusion of her death, then a vow at Nikumbhila, a hymn to the sun, a queen's lament and a funeral, closes on her standing in front of the man she waited for, hearing words she never expected.
screen: `NOT FOR YOU, BUT FOR MY HONOR.` · `GO WHEREVER YOU LIKE.` · `SITA WEEPS.` · `READERS STILL ARGUE.` · then, large: `A WEEK THAT ENDS IN HARD WORDS.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your breath be gentle. Think of a time someone you trusted said something that cut deeper than they knew. You don't need to relive it. Just notice where it still sits in you. Breathe in, and put a kind hand, in your imagination, on that place. Breathe out, and let it be held. Being hurt by words is real. The bell holds the time.
The fire. It begins with Rama's cold words to Sita in front of everyone, a moment readers still argue over.
Your line: the fire. Today, before you speak to someone you love in front of others, think about how it will land. Day six hundred fifty-eight.

fork.setup: you're Sita, rescued after months as a prisoner, walking toward the husband you waited for. he speaks coldly in front of everyone. what do you do?
fork.reveal: Valmiki has her weep first; tomorrow she answers, and her answer is not a plea.

original.note: Sanskrit agni: fire, and Agni, the god of fire, witness of oaths and sacrifices.

trapdoor: what you thought: the war ends, and Rama and Sita embrace.
what it means: Rama speaks coldly in public, and Sita weeps; the reunion becomes a trial.
what a scholar hears: Valmiki's Sanskrit keeps Rama's words unsoftened, and commentators and retellers have offered competing readings of them, none of them final.
